::: {.chapter-goal}
#### In this chapter
You will stop classifying pixels and start classifying objects, removing salt and pepper noise, gaining predictors that pixel based work cannot produce, and delivering vector polygons a planner can open in desktop GIS. You will also learn where the approach makes things worse.
:::

## The problem with the pixel

A ten metre pixel is an arbitrary square. Nothing on the ground is a ten metre square. The boundaries that matter, a stand of mangrove, an aquaculture pond, a plantation block, exist at their own scales and in their own shapes, and imposing a regular grid on them is a convenience of the sensor rather than a property of the landscape.

Two consequences follow, and they are the reasons this chapter exists.

**Salt and pepper noise.** A pixel based classifier decides each pixel independently, so a single anomalous pixel in the middle of a forest gets called water and stays that way. The map is speckled with isolated errors that a human interpreter would never make, because a human uses context.

**Unusable boundaries.** Vectorising a pixel classification produces tens of thousands of ragged squares. Nobody can put that in a management plan.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common failure: smoothing instead of segmenting
The obvious response to salt and pepper is a modal filter, and Chapter [-@sec-supervised] used one. It works, and it is a blunt instrument: it removes noise and real small features indiscriminately, because it cannot tell them apart. A three pixel filter erases an isolated misclassified pixel and an isolated genuine 20 metre mangrove patch with equal enthusiasm. Segmentation addresses the cause; smoothing addresses the symptom.
:::

## What segmentation does

Segmentation groups adjacent pixels that resemble each other into objects, before any classification happens. Each object is then described by its aggregate properties and classified as a unit.

Two things change as a result.

The unit of analysis becomes something that resembles a feature on the ground. Every pixel within an object gets the same class, so isolated errors are impossible by construction.

And a new family of predictors becomes available. A pixel has a value. An object has a mean, a standard deviation, a size, a shape and a perimeter. Standard deviation within an object is the interesting one: a uniform plantation has low internal variance, a structurally complex natural stand has high variance, and the two may have identical means. That is the same insight as the GLCM texture of Chapter [-@sec-texture], arriving by a different route and often more cleanly.

## SNIC, and its three real parameters

Simple Non Iterative Clustering grows superpixels outward from a regular grid of seeds, assigning each pixel to whichever seed it is closest to in a combined spectral and spatial distance. It is fast, deterministic and available in Earth Engine, which is why it is the segmentation algorithm this book uses.

Three parameters do the work, and each is an ecological decision rather than a computational one.

**`size`** sets seed spacing in pixels, and therefore approximate object size. At 10 metre resolution, size 10 produces objects roughly 100 metres across. This is the parameter to think hardest about, because setting it larger than the features you are mapping makes those features disappear inside bigger objects. Over narrow fringing mangrove, small is safer than efficient.

**`compactness`** controls how strongly the algorithm favours regular shapes over following spectral boundaries. Zero lets objects take whatever shape the imagery dictates, which is correct when boundaries are real and irregular, such as a coastline. Higher values produce tidier, more square objects, which suits agricultural fields and suits nothing at all on a delta.

**`connectivity`** is 4 or 8. Eight allows diagonal connection, so objects can follow narrow diagonal features such as tidal creeks. Four is stricter and produces blockier results.

::: {.callout-tip}
## From the field
Set `neighborhoodSize` larger than `size`, usually several times larger. Earth Engine processes in tiles, and if the neighbourhood is too small, objects get cut at tile boundaries and you see a regular grid pattern in the output that has nothing to do with the landscape. It is an easy fix and a confusing symptom.
:::

## Where OBIA wins, and where it makes things worse

This is the honest part, and it is missing from most treatments, which present segmentation as a straightforward upgrade.

**It wins clearly over landscapes with genuine discrete objects.** Agricultural fields, aquaculture ponds, plantation blocks, urban parcels. These are objects on the ground, so making them objects in the analysis aligns the method with the reality. Accuracy usually improves and the cartographic quality improves dramatically.

**It can lose over landscapes with gradational boundaries.** The transition from mangrove to upland forest across an elevation gradient is a gradient, not a line. Segmentation forces a hard boundary somewhere in it, and then commits every pixel in the straddling object to a single answer. A pixel based classifier at least degrades gracefully across the transition, producing a mixed zone that honestly represents an uncertain one.

The practical rule: ask whether the thing you are mapping has edges. If it does, segment. If it fades, be careful, and check the per class accuracy rather than the overall figure, because the loss will be concentrated in exactly the transitional class you care about.

::: {.callout-important}
## Scientific integrity: the minimum mapping unit belongs in the metadata
Filtering out polygons below a threshold is standard cartographic practice and it changes your area statistics. A 0.5 hectare minimum mapping unit removes every fringing stand narrower than a few pixels, which over a delta can be a substantial share of the mangrove extent.

State the minimum mapping unit alongside the scale and the confidence interval from Chapter [-@sec-accuracy]. Two maps of the same coastline reporting different extents have sometimes differed by nothing more than this.
:::

## Vectors as the actual deliverable

There is a practical argument for OBIA with nothing to do with accuracy.

Object boundaries vectorise into clean polygons. A district planner can open them in QGIS, edit them, attach attributes, calculate areas per village, and put the result in a report. That is the form in which geospatial work usually has to arrive to be acted on, and it is worth remembering that Chapter [-@sec-why] defined the whole purpose of the exercise as informing a decision.

A pixel based classification vectorises into a mess. If the deliverable is a shapefile that someone else will work with, segmentation earns its place on that ground alone, even in a landscape where the accuracy gain is zero.

## A hard case: earthquake landslides at Iburi

On 6 September 2018 an earthquake in Hokkaido set off thousands of shallow landslides in a few seconds. This is the landslide exercise from the GEE101 course, rebuilt so you can check each step. It compares the same season a year apart, applies a pixel rule and an object rule, and scores both against a mapped inventory from the CAS Landslide Dataset [@xu2024caslandslide]. Two things in the results are worth more than the maps. First, a fixed threshold fails when the whole scene has shifted. Second, objects are not automatically better than pixels.

{{< include _snippets/ch18_landslide_obia_iburi.qmd >}}

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. Run SNIC at size 5, 10 and 25. Find the size at which a narrow mangrove fringe stops being its own object and gets absorbed into the water.
2. Set compactness to 5 and compare the coastline against compactness 0. Explain in one sentence why compactness suits farmland and not deltas.
3. Compare object and pixel accuracy per class rather than overall. Which classes gained and which lost, and does that match the gradational boundary argument above?
4. Raise the minimum mapping unit to 2 hectares and report how much mangrove area disappeared. That number belongs in your metadata.
5. Export both a pixel based and an object based shapefile and open them in QGIS. Count the polygons in each. That ratio is the practical argument for this chapter.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers

**1.** At `size` 5 (objects about 50 m) a fringe of two or three pixels stays its own object. At 10 (about 100 m) it survives where it is wide, but thin stretches start to merge with the neighbouring object. At 25 (about 250 m) most narrow fringes are absorbed into the water or the inland forest object. The size at which the fringe disappears is roughly the size at which the seed spacing exceeds about twice the fringe width.

**2.** With compactness 5 the objects become rounder and more regular, and the coastline turns into blocky, smoothed shapes that cut across creeks and fringes; with 0 they follow the spectral boundary wherever it goes. One sentence: "Compactness favours regular shapes, which match fields with straight edges but not deltas, where real boundaries are irregular and follow the water."

**3.** Typically the classes with sharp edges and large homogeneous areas (water, ponds, plantations) gain from objects, because salt-and-pepper errors disappear. The classes with gradational boundaries (back-mangrove grading into swamp forest, sparse stands on mudflat) gain little or lose, because an object must pick one class for a mixed transition. If that is your result, it matches the argument in the chapter.

**4.** Compute area with and without the filter: `objects.filter(ee.Filter.gte('area_ha', 2))` versus all objects. Over a delta, raising the minimum mapping unit from 0.5 to 2 ha commonly removes several percent of mangrove area, more where the mangrove is fringing. Report it, for example: "Minimum mapping unit 2 ha; this removed 1,240 ha (3.1 %) of mangrove in patches smaller than 2 ha."

**5.** The pixel-based export, vectorised, produces tens or hundreds of thousands of tiny polygons, many of one or a few pixels. The object-based export produces a few hundred to a few thousand polygons that follow real units. A ratio of 50:1 or more is common. That ratio is what a GIS user, a planner or a field team experiences when they open the file.
:::
